newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai plan to free local sugar raises questions.
newsitem.headline: Thai plan to free local sugar raises questions.

text.p: Thailand's plan to free domestic sugar prices has raised eyebrows and questions from the industry on the possible impact on local and international markets, industry sources said on Monday.
They said the plan, whose details remain sketchy, could make the world sugar market more volatile if not properly executed.

"It is perhaps too early for me to comment as I don't know the full details. But if Thailand is really to liberalise the local sugar market, then world prices could be more volatile because of increased uncertainty over supplies," said a dealer at a foreign trading house.

Thai Cane and Sugar Board secretary general Pramote Vidtayasuk told Reuters on Monday that the board is considering floating its local sugar prices to make it fair to producers and avoid possible shortages caused by millers smuggling out sugar to sell in a more lucrative world market.
However, the details remained vague as Pramote declined to elaborate whether the board planned to scrap the local sugar supply quota or just float prices.

Thailand has pegged local sugar prices at 12.00 baht a kg ($0.39) for white sugar and 13.00 baht for refined sugar since 1981, but the recent currency crisis resulting in the steep fall in the baht against the dollar, has sharply widened the gap with international prices.
The sugar industry is managed by the Thai Cane and Sugar Board which is controlled by the government, millers and sugar cane farmers.

Each year the board sets up a quota for three types of sugar -- the white-only quota A for domestic consumption, the raw-only quota B for export by the Thai Cane and Sugar Corp and quota C comprising both whites and raws to be exported by the private sector.

Thailand's sugar production allocation in the 1996/97 crushing season (November-June) was fixed at around 1.67 million tonnes for quota A, 800,000 tonnes for quota B and around 3.4 million tonnes for quota C.
Pramote said the recent sharp fall in the baht and rising world sugar prices had prompted the board to review local market policy.
The October white sugar futures contract on the London International Financial Futures Exchange (LIFFE) surged $4.30 on Friday to close at $328.50 a tonne.

Although some in the domestic industry said they were pleased with the proposal, as it would represent the first step in the future wholesale liberalisation of the Thai sugar sector, many were cautious and wanted the details to be spelled out soon to assess the short- and medium-term impact of the move.
They questioned what the board's reaction would be if local prices were increased and the baht then firmed and world sugar prices eased.
"Will the prices be really floated? and if so on what basis? Or will the board just raise the prices?," said a local trader.

"If the board just raises local prices, then what will it do to be fair to consumers if world prices drop and the baht firms up. And if the board floats the prices, will farmers and millers accept it if the prices drop," he said.
In the case that local prices are much higher than export prices, sugar is likely to be smuggled into the local market, squeezing world prices up and the opposite could lead to a glut, traders said.
And if the board is to scrap the quota as well, then the small mills will have difficulty competing, they said.
However, milling sources said the most likely scenario is that the board maintains the local quota but floats domestic prices based on international levels.
"That would be the best option. I don't see how the scheme will affect the world market then," said an executive at a major sugar mill here.
